adjudication_records.issue_text: paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result: negative-offset queryset slicing counts from the end of the result set, returning arbitrary wrong rows instead of rows before the offset

paginator.py BasePaginator.get_result: passing negative offsets through to Django slicing causes from-the-end corruption on the base paginator, and the boundary check compares against original `offset` instead of `start_offset`, causing duplicated/dropped rows across page transitions

paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result: the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` prev-boundary check uses the un-clamped offset, so the boundary result is never trimmed when offsets diverge, causing duplicate rows when paging backward

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` block only runs under `if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value`. In that code path, `start_offset` is set to `offset` (unclamped) in the normal branch (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), so there is no “clamped vs unclamped” divergence to cause the boundary check to fail as described. The finding’s premise (offset divergence due to clamping in the prev path) is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result: `if cursor.value:` treats a zero-valued cursor the same as no cursor, so a valid cursor can be ignored and page one silently re-fetched

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the code uses `if cursor.value:` to decide whether to honor the cursor value; a falsy-but-valid value like integer `0` would be treated as “no cursor” and coerced to `cursor_value = 0` (same as the default `Cursor(0,0,0)`). The diff doesn’t prove cursor values can legitimately be numeric zero in real requests (they may be strings like "0", which are truthy), so this is not a clearly verifiable defect from the diff alone, but it is a concrete edge-case in the new logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: cursors.py: no validation constrains client-supplied cursor offsets to be >= 0, allowing crafted negative-offset cursors to pull rows from the end of the queryset and bypass intended traversal order

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly introduces/encourages negative cursor offsets without any validation: `Cursor.__init__` still does `self.offset = int(offset)` with no >=0 constraint, and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` has an `enable_advanced_features` branch that will use `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset` can be negative. Even outside the new paginator, `BasePaginator.get_result()` now allows `offset` to remain negative when `cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). This makes client-crafted negative offsets reachable and can lead to incorrect/unsafe pagination behavior (and in Django ORM commonly results in errors for negative slicing), so the finding that negative offsets are unconstrained is verifiable from the diff (though the exact “pull rows from the end” effect depends on queryset slicing semantics).

adjudication_records.issue_text: organization_auditlogs.py: the `enable_advanced` flag gates users into the broken negative-offset paginator path, so highest-privilege users get broken pagination while ordinary users get working pagination

adjudication.rationale: The optimized path in `organization_auditlogs.py` is gated by `enable_advanced` and passes `enable_advanced_features=True` into `OptimizedCursorPaginator`. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0`, it explicitly sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices/offsets, so a negative `cursor.offset` will raise/break pagination. This failure mode is only reachable for users routed into the optimized paginator (i.e., the gated “advanced” users with `optimized_pagination=true`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative slicing on Django ORM querysets raises ValueError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result and OffsetPaginator.get_result, causing 500 errors for crafted negative-offset cursors
matched_golden_ids: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying bug: the paginator code attempts negative slicing on Django QuerySets, which Django does not support and results in an exception (golden notes AssertionError; candidate notes ValueError) leading to server errors. Candidate adds OffsetPaginator and crafted cursor context, but the core issue matches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: get_item_key rounding direction is inverted vs existing paginators (floor if asc else ceil instead of floor for ascending, ceil for descending), causing duplicated or skipped rows at fractional datetime boundaries

adjudication.rationale: The diff only shows the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` implementation: `floor` when `self._is_asc(for_prev)` else `ceil`. The finding claims the rounding direction is inverted vs existing paginators, but the diff does not show any existing `get_item_key` to compare against, and the described “instead of floor for ascending, ceil for descending” matches what the new code already does. There’s no diff-grounded evidence of an inversion or of fractional-datetime duplication/skipping behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Prev-cursor trimming logic `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` almost never matches with the new start_offset remapping, so the trailing row is not dropped on prev-page navigation, yielding duplicated rows

adjudication.rationale: The `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` trimming check runs only inside `if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value:`. In both modified `get_result` implementations, `start_offset` is only remapped/clamped when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), so for prev-page navigation `start_offset` remains `offset` and the slice bounds are effectively unchanged. Thus the finding’s claim that the new `start_offset` remapping makes the trimming condition “almost never match” on prev navigation isn’t supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Off-by-slice mismatch between start_offset and stop in base paginator when cursor.is_prev is False and offset < 0, causing intended data to be lost; also adds dead/incorrect logic for negative offsets that were never expected

adjudication.rationale: The base paginator change computes `stop` from `start_offset` (`stop = start_offset + limit + extra`), so there’s no verifiable “off-by-slice mismatch” between start and stop. For the cited case (`cursor.is_prev is False` and `offset < 0`), the code explicitly clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset)`, which avoids negative slicing and does not show “intended data lost” in the diff. The finding’s claim about a mismatch/data loss is not supported by what’s changed here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates existing paginator logic with no actual query-level optimization, including the full COUNT(*) count_hits path, adding maintenance burden with no measurable benefit

adjudication.rationale: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` largely reimplements standard paginator flow (cursor defaulting, `build_queryset`, optional `count_hits` via `self.count_hits(max_hits)`, offset/extra handling, reversing for prev, and `build_cursor`) rather than introducing a clear query-level optimization. The only behavioral divergence shown is allowing negative slicing when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, which is not a query optimization per se and adds a parallel codepath to maintain. This is a diff-grounded maintainability/architecture concern rather than a direct correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Audit logs ordered only by -datetime are not uniquely ordered, so cursor pagination can skip or duplicate rows at timestamp boundaries; should use compound ordering ("-datetime", "-id")

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, both the existing and the new optimized pagination paths call `self.paginate(..., order_by="-datetime")` (see both branches). When the optimized path uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (a cursor-based paginator), ordering solely by a non-unique field like `datetime` can make pagination unstable at timestamp ties, causing skipped or duplicated rows at page boundaries. The diff does not add a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g. `-id`), so this correctness issue exists in the newly added cursor-pagination path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Requester-controllable `optimized_pagination=true` query flag selects an entirely different, untested paginator per request, producing inconsistent cursors and 500s when toggled mid-traversal

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a requester-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` flag that switches the endpoint from `DateTimePaginator` to a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (`organization_auditlogs.py`), so cursors/ordering semantics can differ across requests if a client toggles the flag mid-pagination. However, the diff does not show cursor parsing/serialization or any concrete error path proving 500s; the “untested”/“500s” parts aren’t verifiable from the diff alone. This is still a specific, diff-grounded design/compatibility risk introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: organization_context referenced but never defined in get() of organization_auditlogs.py, causing NameError and 500 for all callers of the audit logs endpoint

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` in `organization_auditlogs.py` without showing any definition of `organization_context` in the surrounding added code. If `organization_context` is not an existing parameter/local provided elsewhere in the function/class, this would raise a `NameError` during evaluation (it’s computed unconditionally, before the `if use_optimized...` branch), breaking the endpoint. However, the full `def get(...)` signature/earlier context isn’t shown, so this is likely-but-not-fully-verifiable from the diff excerpt alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New client-controllable query param optimized_pagination=true silently switches pagination mode without versioning or documentation, potentially breaking existing API clients

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new client-controlled query parameter `optimized_pagination` (checked via `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) that conditionally switches the endpoint from `DateTimePaginator` to the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator` for certain users. This is a behavior/API-contract change gated by a query param and not otherwise surfaced in code (e.g., no explicit versioning/feature-flag mechanism shown), which is a concrete review concern. However, it is opt-in and does not affect existing clients unless they send the new param, so it’s not a verifiable defect by itself from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator produces incorrect/empty result sets because Django ORM negative slicing behaves like Python list slicing from the end, breaking cursor ordering invariants

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add negative-offset slicing (e.g., `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset` can be negative in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`). However, the finding’s specific claim that “Django ORM negative slicing behaves like Python list slicing from the end” and thus returns incorrect/empty result sets is not supported by anything shown in the diff, and it misstates Django QuerySet behavior (negative indexing/slicing is generally not supported rather than acting like list-from-end).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-controlled cursor offsets combined with negative slicing allow data exploration beyond intended pagination bounds once advanced features are enabled

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces explicit support for negative `cursor.offset` in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` when `enable_advanced_features` is true: `start_offset = cursor.offset` and `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. `cursor.offset` is derived from the client-controlled cursor (no validation/clamping is shown; `Cursor.__init__` just casts `offset` to `int`). This removes the prior implicit lower-bound behavior (e.g., `max(0, offset)`), so a client can request negative offsets once `optimized_pagination=true` and `enable_advanced` are satisfied, leading to pagination behavior outside normal bounds and potentially unexpected/unsafe traversal semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Changed slicing logic in shared OffsetPaginator.get_result affects all existing endpoints, causing subtle drift in cursor results for reverse pagination (is_prev cursors use unclamped offset and inconsistent filter-first-result bookkeeping)

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetPaginator.get_result`, the new `start_offset` logic only clamps negative offsets when `not cursor.is_prev`; when `cursor.is_prev` it still uses `offset` directly, and `stop` remains `offset + limit + extra` as before. The downstream `is_prev` bookkeeping (`if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value: ...`) is unchanged. So the diff does not show a change that would cause cursor drift specifically for reverse pagination across endpoints.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cursor class does not validate or bounds-check negative offsets, changing the effective input contract of every cursor-paginated API to accept semi-sanctioned negative offsets

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not add any validation in `Cursor.__init__` (it still does `self.offset = int(offset)`), but it newly documents/encourages negative offsets (comment in `sentry/utils/cursors.py`) and adds code paths that may use a negative `cursor.offset` directly in queryset slicing (e.g., `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`: `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`). This raises a real review concern about expanding/implicitly sanctioning negative offsets without explicit bounds/contract enforcement, but the finding’s claim that the Cursor class change itself alters “every cursor-paginated API” overstates what’s shown (it’s mainly the new paginator/logic).

adjudication_records.issue_text: BasePaginator.get_result change alters slicing behavior for all inheriting paginators: the max(0, offset) clamp for non-prev cursors with negative offset silently changes behavior, while prev cursors pass negative offsets through to Django slicing which raises AssertionError or changes query semantics

adjudication.rationale: In `BasePaginator.get_result` the new `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes slicing for all users of this method. For `cursor.is_prev=True`, a negative `cursor.offset` is now passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing (commonly raising `AssertionError`). Meanwhile, non-prev negative offsets are silently clamped to 0, altering behavior from the prior `queryset[offset:stop]` (which would error on negative). The diff also explicitly documents allowing negative offsets (`Cursor.offset` comment), making this crash path plausible.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In BasePaginator.get_result, the elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra check uses the unclamped offset, so when max(0, offset) clamped a negative offset the boundary-trim branch compares against a negative number and never fires, breaking dedup on prev-pagination

adjudication.rationale: In the modified `BasePaginator.get_result`, the offset is only clamped via `start_offset = max(0, offset)` when `not cursor.is_prev`. The boundary-trim/dedup logic that contains `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` is inside `if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value:`, and in that branch `start_offset` is set to `offset` (no clamping). Therefore the described mismatch (clamped `start_offset` vs unclamped `offset` causing the comparison to use a negative number) cannot occur based on this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OptimizedCursorPaginator accepts client-controlled negative offsets with no validation; negative stop values cause exceptions (DoS/500) or read from the end of the queryset, producing silently wrong pagination (duplicate/missing rows with HTTP 200)

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices the Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing and commonly raise errors for negative offsets, causing 500s (DoS potential for any caller who can supply a crafted cursor). The code also lacks validation to prevent negative `offset`/`stop` values; the comment incorrectly assumes the ORM “properly handles negative slicing automatically.” This behavior is newly introduced by the added paginator and its use in `organization_auditlogs` when `optimized_pagination=true` for privileged users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is a non-sequitur justification for negative offset handling; the issue is slicing/cursor math correctness, not access control, and there is no test coverage for the negative-offset path

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the negative-offset branch is justified with a comment about permissions (“safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level”), but the change is about slicing/cursor math, not authorization (diff shows no permission logic tied to slicing). Also, the diff adds a new, nontrivial code path gated by `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0` without adding any accompanying tests in the shown changes (no test files/updates in diff), so correctness of the negative-offset path is unverified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Boundary-trimming logic in OptimizedCursorPaginator is broken for negative offsets: len(results) == offset + limit + extra compares against a negative or unrelated number, causing the elif to fire spuriously (dropping a legitimate row) or never fire (duplicating a boundary row), silently skipping or repeating audit log entries

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the queryset slice uses `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) and `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`, but the boundary-trimming logic later still checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` where `offset` is that negative value. This condition is no longer aligned with how many rows were requested/returned for the slice, so it can fail to trim when needed (or trim inconsistently), potentially causing duplicate or skipped boundary rows during `is_prev` pagination. This mismatch is directly visible in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Hidden undocumented query parameter 'optimized_pagination' switches to a paginator with different correctness semantics, creating a client-controlled silent correctness divergence in the same API contract

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new, client-controlled query param `optimized_pagination` (checked via `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) that switches the endpoint from `DateTimePaginator` to a newly introduced `OptimizedCursorPaginator` only for certain admins (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`). This creates two pagination behaviors/cursor semantics for the same API path depending on an undocumented flag in the request, i.e., a silent divergence in the API contract. The diff itself doesn’t show documentation or explicit contract guarantees, so this is a real review concern but not a strictly verifiable correctness defect on its own.

adjudication_records.issue_text: enable_advanced check may crash: organization_context.member.has_global_access is evaluated without checking the user is a member of the org; if member is None for a non-superuser org-less context it raises AttributeError (500)
matched_golden_ids: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same root bug: code accesses organization_context.member.has_global_access without guarding against organization_context.member being None, leading to an AttributeError/500 in contexts where no org member is present (e.g., API key/org token auth). The candidate omits the optimized_pagination trigger and auth details but identifies the same crashing access pattern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The optimized paginator is triggerable by every user with global access, not restricted to a privileged debug path, changing production behavior for a broad class of users

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly enables the new paginator when `optimized_pagination=true` AND `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` (in `organization_auditlogs.py`). That means any user with `has_global_access` can trigger `OptimizedCursorPaginator` in production via a normal query param, not a debug-only path. This is a real scope/behavior change for a broad set of users, but the diff doesn’t itself prove incorrectness or a security break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: enable_advanced_features kwarg may not survive Endpoint.paginate(), causing TypeError (500) or silent drop of the flag so the feature is dead code that silently does nothing

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get()` passing `enable_advanced_features=True` into `self.paginate(...)`, and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__` accepts that kwarg. However, the diff does not include `Endpoint.paginate()` (or `BaseEndpoint.paginate()`) implementation/signature, so we cannot verify whether it forwards unknown kwargs to the paginator (or would raise a `TypeError` / drop the flag). The finding asserts a concrete runtime failure/dead-code outcome that is not provable from the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: get_item_key floor/ceil math is inverted for descending order compared to established DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator implementations (ceil for asc, floor for desc), which can skip records whose timestamp falls in the rounding gap

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` using `floor` when ascending and `ceil` when descending, but the finding claims this is inverted relative to `DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator`. Those existing implementations are not shown in the diff, so the alleged inversion and its skipping behavior can’t be verified from the provided changes alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: get_item_key passes a datetime to math.floor/ceil which raises TypeError on Python 3, causing the first non-empty page to 500 since the paginator is used with the datetime key ordered by '-datetime'

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` which does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `math.floor/ceil(value)` before casting to `int`. In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new path uses `paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`, which implies `self.key` will be `"datetime"` and `value` will be a `datetime`. `math.floor/ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError` on Python 3, so enabling `optimized_pagination=true` for an allowed user would 500 on the first non-empty page.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Prev-trim elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra is dead/unreachable in the normal path when offset > 0, since len(results) is capped at limit + extra and can never equal offset + limit + extra, leaving duplicate boundary rows untrimmed across pages

adjudication.rationale: In both the existing `get_result` logic and the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the prev-trim branch `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` appears effectively unreachable when `offset > 0`. In the normal slicing path, `results` comes from `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`, so `len(results)` is capped at `limit + extra`, while the RHS is `offset + limit + extra` (> `limit + extra` if `offset > 0`). This makes that condition dead for positive offsets, suggesting the trimming logic is at least inconsistent/suspicious, though the claimed duplicate-row impact isn’t directly provable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Duplicated code path in OptimizedCursorPaginator is byte-identical to BasePaginator logic except for the missing clamp; the change provides no measurable performance benefit while removing a safety clamp, with no benchmark or tests justifying it

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that substantially duplicates the existing pagination logic (offset/extra/stop slicing, prev handling, reversing, `build_cursor`, and `post_query_filter`). The main behavioral delta is the new branch that allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, i.e. it intentionally bypasses the clamping (`max(0, offset)`) used elsewhere. The finding’s claim about “no measurable performance benefit”/lack of benchmarks can’t be verified from the diff, but the duplication and removal/bypass of the clamp are directly evidenced by the added code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cursor.__init__ accepts arbitrary negative offsets with no range validation at the single chokepoint where it could be enforced; validation was instead scattered and inconsistently clamped downstream

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly leaves `Cursor.offset = int(offset)` in `src/sentry/utils/cursors.py` with no range validation while adding comments endorsing negative offsets. Downstream handling is inconsistent: `DateTimePaginator.get_result` now clamps `offset` only when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), meaning a negative `cursor.offset` with `is_prev=True` will slice `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative start. The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` even deliberately allows negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is set (`start_offset = cursor.offset`), again leading to negative queryset slicing. This is a concrete correctness risk introduced/exposed by the diff and aligns with the finding that validation isn’t enforced at the single chokepoint and is inconsistently handled downstream.

adjudication_records.issue_text: hits/count_hits handling in OptimizedCursorPaginator is dead/redundant boilerplate copied from an ancestor with subtly different semantics, indicating copy-paste drift in pagination logic

adjudication.rationale: In the added `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result(...)`, the `count_hits/known_hits/max_hits` logic is not dead: it computes `hits` and passes it into `build_cursor(...)` (`hits=hits`, `max_hits=...`). The diff does not show any “subtly different semantics” vs an ancestor, nor does it show that this code is redundant/unreachable; it’s plausible `paginate()` uses these parameters even if the shown endpoint doesn’t. The finding asserts copy-paste drift that can’t be verified from the diff.
